record.paper_title: Cyber-Physical Attacks on UAS Networks–Challenges and Open Research Problems
record.context_brief: Routing convergence disruption in UAS networks
record.original_question: Can adversaries feasibly prevent or slow routing convergence in UAS networks by combining topological perturbation, jamming or adaptive-formation exploitation, and manipulation of node geographical-position knowledge, and what countermeasures can protect convergence in hostile airborne-network environments?

evidence.quote: Mobile routing in UAS networks is a surface for attacks on convergence of the network. As discussed, the topology of unmanned airborne networks is subject to manipulation by adversarial actions such as exploitation of adaptive formation control and jamming attacks. Also, many of the recently proposed routing mechanisms for airborne networks rely on global knowledge of the geographical positions of every node in the network, which may also be prone to manipulation.

A sophisticated adversary may be able to design a strategic combination of topological perturbation and sensor manipulations to prevent or slow the convergence of routing in the network. Investigation of this attack in terms of feasibility, as well as potential countermeasures may prove to be valuable for efficient protection of UAS networks operating in hostile environments.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a mobile airborne network modeled as a time-varying graph G(t) = (V, E(t)), where V is a set of unmanned aerial nodes whose positions p_v(t) ∈ R^3 evolve under an adaptive formation-control law, and E(t) is determined by a communication range and channel availability. Each node v maintains an estimate of the geographical positions {p̂_u(t)}_{u∈V} used by a position-based routing protocol R that converges (in the absence of attacks) to a stable forwarding configuration after a finite time T_conv.

Suppose an adversary may, within bounded resources, simultaneously perform any combination of the following actions:
(i) topological perturbation — forcing or removing a bounded number of edges in E(t) per time unit,
(ii) jamming — denying communication on a bounded subset of links or frequencies,
(iii) formation exploitation — injecting control-input perturbations of bounded magnitude that drive the formation-control dynamics so as to alter G(t),
(iv) position manipulation — corrupting the position estimates p̂_u(t) at a bounded number of nodes by bounded offsets.

Address the following:

1. Establish necessary and sufficient conditions on the adversary's resource bounds under which there exists an attack strategy that prevents the routing protocol R from converging, or forces its convergence time to exceed any prescribed threshold T* with high probability.

2. Construct, when feasible, an explicit such adversarial strategy combining (i)–(iv), and characterize its computational complexity.

3. Design a routing/defense mechanism R' (e.g., based on robust position verification, redundant topology maintenance, or anti-jamming coding) and prove quantitative guarantees on the convergence time of R' under the same adversarial model, identifying the largest adversary budget that R' can tolerate.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research problem on convergence attacks against routing in unmanned airborne networks. No published source was found that provides a complete formal feasibility characterization together with provably resilient countermeasures matching the combined adversary model (topology + jamming + formation exploitation + position manipulation). The problem appears to remain open.
